paragraphs: A/B tests compare outcomes between treatment groups, but networked users can make those comparisons harder to interpret. Connected users often behave similarly, and users’ individual characteristics can also predict their outcomes. This paper studies how random assignment can account for both sources of structure when estimating an average treatment effect.

The authors propose an adaptive randomization procedure that balances user characteristics and network information together. Its theoretical guarantee states that the corresponding imbalance measures are bounded in probability, expressed as O_p(1). This describes controlled imbalance rather than requiring the two groups to match perfectly on every characteristic or network feature.

The paper also connects better balance to greater estimation efficiency, measured through mean squared error. Numerical studies find more comparable treatment groups and lower error in estimating the average treatment effect. The contribution therefore links the design of treatment assignment to the quality of the resulting estimate: network information and individual characteristics can both help make the comparison more precise.
icml-2023-a-b-testing-in-network-data-wi.tldr: An adaptive randomization procedure balances network information and user characteristics to improve average treatment effect estimation in network A/B tests.

paragraphs: Self-supervised pretraining has produced strong results for large vision transformers, but its value for smaller versions is less established. This paper develops and compares several pretraining methods for lightweight vision transformers, evaluating them on image classification and downstream tasks that require predictions across an image.

The central finding is that suitable pretraining allows even plain lightweight transformers to match the performance of earlier leading networks with carefully engineered architectures. This challenges the view that standard transformer designs are inherently unsuitable at small sizes. However, the authors also identify shortcomings: the studied pretraining does not benefit from larger pretraining datasets and performs less well when downstream data are scarce.

To understand these outcomes, the authors examine representations within network layers and the models’ attention maps. Those analyses motivate a distillation strategy applied during pretraining. It further improves downstream performance for masked-autoencoder-based pretraining. Together, the results show that pretraining choices deserve attention alongside architecture design, while identifying specific settings where the studied methods remain less effective.
icml-2023-a-closer-look-at-self-supervis.tldr: Suitable self-supervised pretraining makes plain lightweight vision transformers competitive, and an analysis-guided distillation strategy further improves masked-autoencoder pretraining.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through discrete firing events and can be energy efficient on neuromorphic hardware. Their all-or-none spikes, however, prevent ordinary backpropagation through the firing operation. Existing surrogate-gradient methods use smooth substitutes, but a fixed amount of smoothing introduces error into the estimated gradients.

The proposed approach makes the amount of relaxation learnable and combines it with random spike noise. Training begins with a prototype network and gradually evolves toward training a spiking network. This gives the optimization process a way to adjust its approximation instead of using the same smoothing throughout. The theoretical analysis shows how optimization of the noisy network can progressively become optimization of an embedded spiking network sharing its weights.

Experiments cover static images, dynamic event streams, speech, and instrumental sounds. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated datasets and strong robustness to different relaxation degrees. These findings support adapting the smoothing during training as a practical way to address the mismatch between continuous gradient calculations and discrete spike behavior.
icml-2023-adaptive-smoothing-gradient-le.tldr: Learning the amount of gradient smoothing lets training progressively approach a spiking network, with strong reported results across several data types.

paragraphs: A Go system can outperform human players yet still make severe mistakes against a deliberately chosen opponent. This paper trains adversarial policies against KataGo to uncover such weaknesses. The resulting opponents achieve a win rate above 97% against KataGo operating at settings described as superhuman.

The adversaries succeed by provoking serious blunders rather than through generally strong Go play. Their attack also transfers to other superhuman Go systems without additional training against those systems. Human experts can understand the strategy well enough to implement it without algorithmic assistance and consistently defeat superhuman opponents. This makes the discovered weakness accessible through a human-executable strategy as well as a trained policy.

The authors further report that the core vulnerability remains in KataGo agents adversarially trained to resist the attack. These results establish a concrete separation between exceptional playing strength and resistance to targeted exploitation. They show that superhuman performance can coexist with surprising failure modes, including one that the reported defensive training does not eliminate.
icml-2023-adversarial-policies-beat-supe.tldr: Trained adversarial opponents beat superhuman KataGo by provoking blunders, with attacks that transfer to other Go AIs and can be executed by human experts.

paragraphs: This paper studies online optimization with bandit feedback for a class of functions exhibiting diminishing returns. The learner must make repeated choices while receiving limited feedback about their value. The authors focus on monotone, multilinear DR-submodular functions and introduce an algorithm called BanditMLSM.

BanditMLSM achieves O(T^(2/3) log T) regret relative to a benchmark scaled by 1−1/e, where T is the number of rounds. That approximation factor is part of the guarantee: the comparison is to a fraction of the optimum. Because the regret grows more slowly than T, its contribution per round decreases as the interaction continues.

The authors then reduce two other problems to this framework: submodular bandits with partition matroid constraints and sequential monotone maximization with bandit feedback. Both inherit the same guarantee. They describe the first result as, to their knowledge, the first sublinear-regret algorithm for the general partition-constrained problem. For sequential maximization, the result improves the approximation factor from the previously reported 1/2 to 1−1/e, while introducing a logarithmic factor in the stated regret rate.
icml-2023-bandit-multi-linear-dr-submodu.tldr: BanditMLSM provides sublinear approximation regret for diminishing-returns optimization and transfers its guarantee to two constrained bandit problems.

paragraphs: Neurons can interact through many recurring connection patterns, called circuit motifs. This paper argues that neural network architectures restricted to only a few such patterns may vary substantially in performance across tasks. CircuitNet is designed to support a broader range of connections within one general architecture.

Its basic building block is a densely connected group of neurons called a circuit motif unit. Adjusting weights inside these units allows them to model different motifs, including feedback and lateral connections beyond those available in traditional feed-forward networks. Connections between units are sparse and pass through designated input and output ports, supporting several rounds of signal transmission.

This design combines dense local interaction with sparse communication across the network. Experiments show that CircuitNet can outperform popular architectures on function approximation, reinforcement learning, image classification, and time series forecasting. The findings support the usefulness of flexible connectivity across several task types. The architectural contribution is a reusable unit whose internal weights can express varied interaction patterns while participating in a larger sparsely connected system.
icml-2023-circuitnet-a-generic-neural-ne.tldr: CircuitNet combines dense, flexible circuit units with sparse connections between them and reports improvements across several kinds of learning tasks.

paragraphs: In a zero-sum game, one player’s improvement comes at the other player’s expense, so optimization must account for their interaction. This paper introduces competitive gradient optimization, or CGO, whose iterative updates explicitly incorporate interactions between the two players. The initial objective is convergence to stationary points, where the relevant gradients vanish.

The authors analyze CGO in both continuous and discrete time. Their continuous-time analysis examines its convergence behavior and shows that previous methods reduce to variants of gradient descent ascent in the continuous limit. For discrete updates, they also establish a convergence rate to stationary points, giving a guarantee directly relevant to an iterative algorithm.

Stronger conclusions require additional structure. The paper defines a generalized class of alpha-coherent functions and proves that CGO converges to a saddle point for strictly alpha-coherent functions. An optimistic variant, oCGO, achieves an O(1/n) rate to saddle points for alpha-coherent functions. These results distinguish reaching a stationary point from reaching a saddle point and make the structural conditions behind the latter guarantees explicit.
icml-2023-competitive-gradient-optimizat.tldr: CGO incorporates player interactions into zero-sum optimization and provides stationary-point and conditional saddle-point convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation summarizes how data are distributed, but adding differential privacy can make that computation expensive. Earlier private algorithms for the Gaussian kernel had running times exponential in the number of dimensions. This paper develops private approximations whose running time depends linearly on dimension, addressing a major obstacle for high-dimensional data.

The main tool is a general framework called Locality Sensitive Quantization. It allows existing techniques for approximating kernel densities to be converted into private mechanisms through a black-box construction. The authors apply this framework to Random Fourier Features, the Fast Gauss Transform, and Locality Sensitive Hashing, connecting private estimation to several established computational approaches.

The paper also improves theoretical bounds for low-dimensional data, so the contribution extends beyond changing the high-dimensional dependence. Experiments report fast and accurate private density estimates on large datasets in both dimensional regimes. Together, the results show how a reusable conversion framework can preserve useful computational advantages of non-private approximation methods while supplying differential privacy.
icml-2023-fast-private-kernel-density-es.tldr: Locality Sensitive Quantization converts existing density approximation methods into private mechanisms with linear rather than exponential dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization selects the settings used to train a model, and benchmarks make it easier to study methods for performing that selection. This paper focuses on federated learning, where models are learned collaboratively from dispersed data. The authors argue that benchmarks built for traditional learning do not adequately serve this setting.

They first examine what distinguishes federated hyperparameter optimization from its conventional counterpart. Based on those differences, they implement FedHPO-Bench, a benchmark suite containing a broad collection of federated optimization problems. The suite permits flexible customization of function evaluations and is designed to accommodate further extensions as research needs develop.

The authors also conduct extensive experiments using the suite to provide insights into federated hyperparameter optimization. The contribution combines a study of the setting with shared experimental infrastructure. Customizable evaluations and extensibility matter because a useful benchmark must support investigation of the federated problem itself, rather than simply reuse an evaluation setup intended for a different learning paradigm. The suite is released as open-source software.
icml-2023-fedhpo-bench-a-benchmark-suite.tldr: FedHPO-Bench provides customizable, extensible benchmarks for studying hyperparameter optimization in federated learning.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent interactions involving groups of entities, making them useful when relationships extend beyond pairs. Many hypergraph neural networks adapt architectures from ordinary graph neural networks. This paper develops a different starting point: a family of learnable energy functions that incorporate hypergraph structure.

Minimizing one of these energies produces representations for the nodes. A parameterized classifier then uses those representations to make predictions. The energy function and classifier are trained together through supervised bilevel optimization, meaning that the prediction-learning process includes an inner optimization that determines the node representations. This connects the representations directly to both the hypergraph and the supervised prediction objective.

The authors also explain parallels between the architecture implicit in this optimization process and commonly used graph neural networks. Their experiments report state-of-the-art results on several hypergraph node classification benchmarks. The work therefore contributes both a way to construct predictive models from energy minimization and evidence that the resulting models can perform strongly on the evaluated tasks.
icml-2023-from-hypergraph-energy-functio.tldr: Learnable hypergraph energy functions generate node representations through optimization, producing models with strong reported node-classification results.

paragraphs: Choosing a learning rate strongly affects how an optimization algorithm converges. The Polyak step size offers an adaptive choice for gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent without estimating the objective’s smoothness parameter. This paper addresses how to extend that principle systematically to methods that also use momentum.

The authors develop a general framework motivated by the derivation of the Polyak rule. It adjusts step sizes for first-order methods with momentum rather than treating the learning rate and momentum behavior as unrelated choices. The resulting techniques are reported to be much less sensitive to the momentum parameter and may avoid heavy-ball oscillations on ill-conditioned problems.

The framework is also extended to stochastic optimization, providing adaptive choices for stochastic gradient descent with momentum. On large-scale machine learning tasks, the proposed methods are demonstrated to be more effective than earlier adaptive step-size algorithms for stochastic gradient methods. The contribution is thus a principled route from an established adaptive rule to momentum-based training, with reported benefits for parameter sensitivity and practical effectiveness.
icml-2023-generalized-polyak-step-size-f.tldr: A generalized Polyak framework adapts learning rates for momentum methods, reducing momentum sensitivity and improving reported stochastic optimization performance.

paragraphs: When a target task has little data, learning shared representations from source tasks can help. The practical question is which sources to sample and how much data to obtain from each. This paper studies that selection problem, including situations where training on a sparse set of sources is desirable.

The authors replace an earlier strategy based on L2-regularized target–source relevance with one based on L1-regularized relevance. They establish a lower bound for the earlier strategy to demonstrate the theoretical dominance of the new approach in source sample complexity. This connects the choice of relevance measure to how many source examples the learner needs.

Because the new relevance parameter may be unknown, the paper proposes estimating it with LASSO. The resulting algorithm recovers the optimal result available when that parameter is known. The authors also analyze the strategy’s potential when source samples have associated costs and provide experiments on real-world computer vision datasets. Together, these contributions address both the statistical efficiency of source selection and its practical use when relevance must be learned.
icml-2023-improved-active-multi-task-rep.tldr: An L1-based source-task selection strategy, estimated with LASSO, improves theoretical sample efficiency in active multi-task representation learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often learn each task from scratch, which uses substantial interaction data. Training on many tasks can help, but transferring to tasks outside that training distribution remains difficult. This paper investigates whether learning an environment model helps agents reuse knowledge and why such a benefit arises.

The authors compare model-based agents with controlled model-free baselines and find better transfer from the model-based approach. Ablation studies indicate that successful transfer depends on both the policy and the dynamics model learned through exploration. The result attributes value to the combination of learned behavior and knowledge about how the environment changes.

Experiments span three transfer settings: procedural tasks within the distribution in Crafter, identical environments within the distribution in RoboDesk, and out-of-distribution tasks in Meta-World. Across these settings, the findings support combining intrinsic exploration with environment models as a viable direction for self-supervised agents that adapt to new reward functions. The evidence concerns transfer across these tested domains and highlights which learned components contribute to it.
icml-2023-investigating-the-role-of-mode.tldr: Controlled experiments show that exploration-trained policies and dynamics models both contribute to stronger model-based transfer.

paragraphs: An agent may already have a dataset of past experience while still being allowed to interact with its environment. This paper asks how that dataset can reduce the additional interactions needed to learn a policy within epsilon of optimal. It names this combined setting FineTuneRL and studies Markov decision processes with linear structure.

The authors characterize the number of online samples necessary given an offline dataset and introduce FTPedel, an algorithm that is provably optimal up to factors involving H. This provides a theoretical account of how existing data change the remaining learning requirement. An explicit example shows that combining stored experience with new interactions can provably improve on either purely offline or purely online learning.

The analysis also distinguishes verifiable learning, typically considered in online reinforcement learning, from the unverifiable learning often considered offline. It proves a formal separation between these regimes. That distinction matters when interpreting what it means to succeed with existing data: the learning requirement includes whether success must be verifiable, alongside the quality of the policy obtained.
icml-2023-leveraging-offline-data-in-onl.tldr: For linearly structured MDPs, FTPedel nearly optimally combines offline data with online interaction, with a provable example of gains over either alone.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms must decide when to choose an apparently rewarding option and when to gather more information. For complex reward models, that exploration decision is difficult because uncertainty often has no convenient analytical expression. This paper introduces Multiplier Bootstrap-based Exploration, or MBE, as a broadly applicable exploration strategy.

Its stated requirement is that the reward model can be trained by minimizing a weighted loss. That gives the method a concrete compatibility criterion and avoids tying its applicability to a particular analytical uncertainty formula. The contribution is therefore relevant to models for which fitting is available even when a direct uncertainty calculation is difficult.

The authors prove rate-optimal regret bounds for sub-Gaussian multi-armed bandits, both for bounds that depend on the particular problem instance and for bounds that do not. These theoretical guarantees apply to that specified bandit setting. Extensive simulations and real-data experiments additionally demonstrate the method’s generality and adaptivity. The paper combines a flexible interface for reward modeling with optimal-rate theory in a defined setting and broader empirical evidence.
icml-2023-multiplier-bootstrap-based-exp.tldr: MBE supports exploration with reward models trained by weighted loss minimization and achieves optimal regret rates in sub-Gaussian multi-armed bandits.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, as its objective and tau as the risk-tolerance parameter. It asks how much regret is unavoidable and designs efficient algorithms approaching those limits. The analysis begins with multi-armed bandits before extending to tabular Markov decision processes.

For bandits with A actions and K episodes, the authors establish a minimax regret rate of order sqrt(AK/tau). An upper-confidence-bound algorithm using a new Bernstein bonus achieves that rate. For tabular reinforcement learning with S states and normalized cumulative rewards, they establish a lower bound of order sqrt(SAK/tau) and propose a bonus-based value iteration procedure.

The reinforcement learning procedure matches that dependence up to logarithmic factors under a continuity assumption. In general, its bound is instead of order sqrt(SAK)/tau, again up to logarithmic factors, and is minimax-optimal for constant tau. The distinction makes clear where the stronger risk-tolerance dependence requires additional structure. Appropriate reward discretization also makes the proposed algorithms computationally efficient.
icml-2023-near-minimax-optimal-risk-sens.tldr: New CVaR learning algorithms attain optimal bandit regret and near-optimal tabular RL regret, with stronger RL guarantees under a continuity assumption.

paragraphs: A generative model may produce an output substantially similar to copyrighted material in its training data. This paper develops a formal way to bound that probability, even when the material was included during training. The proposed property is called near access-freeness, or NAF.

Roughly, a model is k-NAF when its output distribution differs by at most k bits from that of a comparison model that never accessed the protected item. This comparison makes the protection relative to a model without access to that item. The authors prove probability bounds for generating similar content when the NAF condition holds.

The paper also provides algorithms that efficiently modify a generative-model learning procedure in a black-box manner to obtain strong bounds on sampling protected content. Experiments with transformer language models and diffusion image models are described as promising, with minimal loss of output quality alongside strong protection. The contribution joins a precise probabilistic definition, learning procedures designed to satisfy protective bounds, and empirical evidence about the resulting quality tradeoff.
icml-2023-on-provable-copyright-protecti.tldr: Near access-freeness bounds protected-content generation by comparing a model with one that never accessed the protected item.

paragraphs: Prior knowledge can be expressed as rules restricting which labels are consistent with one another. This paper compares two ways to use such constraints: encouraging compliance during training through regularization and enforcing constraints when making predictions. It analyzes how each choice affects model performance.

Constraint-based regularization excludes models inconsistent with the rules, which narrows the gap between training and generalization performance. However, favoring small violations also introduces a bias toward a suboptimal model. Constrained inference has a different effect: by correcting violations in a model’s predictions, it reduces population risk. In that sense, violations provide opportunities for correction at prediction time.

The authors then study using both approaches together. They propose conditions under which constrained inference can compensate for the bias introduced by regularization, aiming to improve model complexity and optimal risk simultaneously. The contribution explains why the stage at which a rule is applied matters. Restricting model learning and correcting predictions have distinct statistical effects, and their combination benefits from conditions that account for those differences.
icml-2023-on-regularization-and-inferenc.tldr: The paper analyzes how label constraints affect training and inference differently and gives conditions for inference corrections to offset regularization bias.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning can draw on datasets containing examples contributed by users or gathered from open sources. This paper studies how adversarial contributions to those datasets can change a language model’s behavior. The targeted effect appears when a chosen trigger phrase occurs in a later input, potentially disrupting several kinds of tasks.

The authors construct poisoned examples by optimizing their inputs and outputs using a bag-of-words approximation to the language model. They evaluate the approach on open-source instruction-tuned models. With as few as 100 poisoned examples, the reported attacks make arbitrary phrases consistently negative or produce degenerate outputs across hundreds of held-out tasks.

The experiments also find increasing vulnerability in larger models. Defenses based on filtering training data or reducing model capacity provide only moderate protection while lowering test accuracy. These findings show that a small contribution to instruction-tuning data can have effects extending across many downstream tasks. They also identify a tradeoff in the evaluated defenses: reducing the attack’s impact comes with a loss in ordinary task performance.
icml-2023-poisoning-language-models-duri.tldr: As few as 100 poisoned instruction-tuning examples cause trigger-dependent failures across many held-out tasks in the evaluated open-source language models.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes seek reliable policies when the environment model contains errors. Policy-gradient methods are widely useful in reinforcement learning, but adapting them to robust decision processes has proved difficult. This paper introduces Double-Loop Robust Policy Gradient, or DRPG, described as the first generic policy-gradient method for this setting.

A central feature is that DRPG steadily reduces approximation errors during optimization. The authors use that property to guarantee convergence to a globally optimal policy in tabular robust Markov decision processes. The tabular scope is part of the guarantee: it specifies the setting in which the claimed global result holds.

The method introduces a new parameterized transition kernel and uses a gradient-based procedure to solve the robust policy problem in its inner loop. Numerical experiments demonstrate the algorithm’s utility and support its global convergence properties. The work connects a practical family of policy optimization methods to robust decision-making, with explicit control of approximation errors providing the basis for the theoretical convergence result.
icml-2023-policy-gradient-in-robust-mdps.tldr: DRPG controls approximation errors to guarantee convergence to a globally optimal policy in tabular robust Markov decision processes.

paragraphs: One-shot neural architecture search trains many candidate networks through shared weights. A very large candidate space can weaken individual subnetworks and make finding a suitable final model expensive. This paper introduces PreNAS, which focuses the shared training process on a smaller set of preferred architectures.

Before training, a zero-cost selector dramatically reduces the candidate space. Weight-sharing training then concentrates on those selected architectures, with the aim of reducing conflicts between their updates. This changes where the architecture-selection effort enters the process: preferred models are identified in advance so training can emphasize them and later specialization requires no search.

Experiments cover both vision transformer and convolutional architectures. The authors report that PreNAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art one-shot search competitors in those evaluations and enables instant specialization with zero search cost. That search-cost claim concerns specialization; the method still performs shared training. The contribution connects improved subnet performance with a more focused training space, while removing the subsequent search step used to choose a specialized model.
icml-2023-prenas-preferred-one-shot-lear.tldr: PreNAS selects preferred architectures before shared training, improving reported performance and enabling specialization without a subsequent search.

paragraphs: Learning to imitate from images or video requires separating useful information from visual distractions. Model-based imitation learning can use high-dimensional observations efficiently, but existing methods can be misled by task-irrelevant content, particularly moving distractors. This paper proposes SeMAIL to address that problem through the structure of its environment model.

SeMAIL separates environment dynamics into two parts according to their task-relevant dependence on the agent’s actions and trains the parts separately. The agent then imagines trajectories and imitates expert behavior within the task-relevant state space. The separation is intended to keep irrelevant visual changes from dominating the model used to learn the behavior.

The authors report near-expert performance on several visual control tasks with complex observations. They also evaluate harder tasks where the learner’s backgrounds differ from those in the expert observations. Those results support separating the modeled dynamics as a way to make visual imitation less vulnerable to distractors. The approach ties the representation used for imagined experience to action-related task structure.
icml-2023-semail-eliminating-distractors.tldr: SeMAIL separates task-relevant and irrelevant dynamics so visual imitation can focus on expert behavior despite distracting or changed backgrounds.

paragraphs: In a streaming bandit problem, a learner encounters options under memory constraints and must choose which ones to play. This paper studies the single-pass setting and asks for the best achievable regret when memory is smaller than the number of arms. Here, K counts arms and T counts trials.

The authors strengthen the lower bound for algorithms using o(K) memory to order K^(1/3)T^(2/3). They then construct algorithms achieving the same order of expected regret with memory for at most O(log-star K) arms. Their construction uses streaming algorithms for finding an approximately best arm and removes a logarithmic factor present in the previous best upper bound.

Matching the lower and upper bounds closes the stated theoretical gap, identifying the achievable regret scale under the memory constraint. Simulations also compare the proposed methods with uniform exploration. The new algorithms outperform that benchmark by a large margin in the reported experiments, sometimes reducing regret by as much as 70%. This empirical finding complements the matching asymptotic guarantees.
icml-2023-tight-regret-bounds-for-single.tldr: Matching lower and upper bounds establish optimal-order regret for single-pass streaming bandits using very little arm memory.

paragraphs: Additive models offer flexible predictions while retaining an interpretable structure, but training them to minimize average loss may be unsuitable for some problems. This paper highlights complex non-Gaussian noise and imbalanced labels as motivating cases. It proposes sparse additive models trained through tilted empirical risk minimization.

Tilting changes how individual losses influence the training objective. This gives the model family flexibility to address variable selection, robust estimation, imbalanced classification, and multiple learning objectives. The contribution changes the criterion used to fit the additive model, allowing the influence of examples to reflect goals that ordinary average-loss minimization may handle poorly.

The authors provide a learning-theoretic analysis centered on generalization and function-approximation error bounds, with the latter established under specific data distributions. They also design an accelerated optimization method combining Prox-SVRG with a random Fourier acceleration technique. Experiments on synthetic and real data report competitive performance. The work therefore develops the modeling objective, its theoretical analysis, and an optimization procedure together, with empirical assessments supporting its practical use.
icml-2023-tilted-sparse-additive-models-.tldr: Tilted sparse additive models adjust the influence of individual losses to support robust, imbalanced, and multiobjective learning.

paragraphs: Removing channels can compress a neural network, yet a smaller model is not always faster. In networks with multiple branches, pruning can introduce memory copies during inference and increase latency. Conventional pruning constraints avoid those copies by removing certain channels together, but the authors show that these restrictions can substantially hurt accuracy.

UPSCALE addresses the tradeoff by reordering channels when the model is exported. Reordering reduces memory copies while allowing the pruning method to choose channels without the conventional grouping constraints. The authors build a generic algorithm supporting any pruning pattern, connecting the choice of which channels to remove with how the resulting model is arranged for execution.

Removing constraints from existing pruners improves ImageNet accuracy for post-training pruned models by 2.1 points on average in the reported results, with gains also highlighted for DenseNet, EfficientNetV2, and ResNet. Channel reordering improves inference speed by up to twofold over a baseline export. These findings show why compression decisions and exported memory layout need to be considered together.
icml-2023-upscale-unconstrained-channel-.tldr: UPSCALE reorders channels at export time to reduce memory copies and enable unconstrained pruning with reported accuracy and speed gains.
